title: Failure and recovery: an alert storm with no grouping

steps.n: A shared storage volume reaches 100 percent.
Twenty-nine services that use the volume begin to fail.
Two hundred alerts reach the pager in ten minutes.
The engineer spends the early minutes reading alerts one by one.
The common dependency is finally spotted and space is freed.
The failing services recover and the dependent alerts clear.
Stable labels, grouping by dependency and inhibition rules are added for next time.

title: Failure and recovery: a cleanup that deleted too much

steps.n: A cleanup rule runs when the disk is nearly full.
A path variable is empty, so the delete scope is far wider than intended.
Files other services need are deleted and errors begin.
The team stops all automation with one control.
The latest snapshot is mounted and files are restored and verified.
The rule now aborts on an empty target and deletes only inside a named directory.

steps.l: Add limits and a dry run
steps.n: Action limits, a dry run, verification and an audit log are added to every rule.

title: How a guest starts on KVM
summary: From virsh start to a running guest.

steps.n: The admin asks libvirt to start the guest defined in its XML file, which lists CPUs, memory, disks and network interfaces.
libvirt checks that the disks exist, the network is defined and the host has memory to give the guest.
libvirt starts a QEMU process with the devices from the definition. QEMU provides the virtual hardware.
QEMU asks the kernel KVM module for a virtual machine and virtual CPUs, which run guest code directly on the real CPU.
QEMU opens the disk image and connects the virtual network card to the bridge on the host.
The virtual CPUs begin executing firmware, which loads the guest kernel from the virtual disk.
The guest gets an address and answers on the network. From the host it is one QEMU process with its own memory.

title: A live migration
summary: Copy memory while the guest keeps running.

steps.n: The admin asks the source host to migrate the guest to the destination, over shared storage or with disk copy.
The destination starts an empty guest of the same shape and waits for memory pages to arrive.
The source copies every memory page to the destination while the guest keeps running.
The running guest changes some pages, so they must be copied again in later rounds.
Each round copies fewer pages if the network is faster than the guest writes. The rounds stop when the rest is small.
The source pauses the guest for a moment, sends the last pages and CPU state, and the destination resumes it.
The guest continues with its address and sessions. The source releases its memory.

title: Failure and recovery: a pool full of snapshots
summary: Overlays grow until the pool fills and guests pause.

steps.n: Each guest with snapshots writes changes into an overlay file, which grows with every write.
Twelve snapshot chains grow for a week and the pool passes 90 percent with no alert.
A guest write cannot allocate a block, so the hypervisor gets an error from the pool.
To protect data the hypervisor pauses affected guests with an I/O error. Users see hung services.
Application monitoring reports failures. The on-call engineer sees paused guests, not the cause.
virsh pool-info shows no space left and virsh snapshot-list shows old snapshots on every guest.
After confirming backups, the engineer deletes the oldest snapshots one guest at a time and watches the pool.
With free space, the guests resume. Later the team adds snapshot expiry and an alert at 80 percent.

title: A write from program to disk

steps.n: The program writes bytes. The kernel copies them into the page cache and the call returns quickly.
The pages are dirty: newer in memory than on disk. They will be written later in the background.
A database calls fsync to demand that the data is safe on disk before it carries on.
The filesystem first records the intended change in its journal so a crash can be repaired.
The filesystem hands the data blocks to the block layer, which queues and merges requests.
The disk stores the blocks, and a flush makes sure its own cache is on stable media.
Only now does the call return. A crash after this point cannot lose the data.
The admin runs vgs to see whether the volume group has free space, and adds a new disk with vgextend if not.
The command enlarges the logical volume by taking free extents from the group.
With the resize option the tool runs the filesystem growth for you after the volume has grown.
ext4 or XFS adds the new space to its structures while it stays mounted and in use.
df now shows the larger size, and applications carry on without restarting.
The admin checks lsblk, df and the application logs, and records the change.

title: Failure and recovery: a bad fstab line stops boot
summary: One wrong UUID sends the server to emergency mode.

steps.n: The admin adds a data disk to fstab, copying the UUID by hand and making one character wrong.
The server is restarted without testing the file with mount -a.
During boot systemd turns every line into a mount unit, including the new one.
The UUID matches no device, so the mount unit waits and then fails.
Because the mount is required, boot stops and the console shows an emergency prompt.
The admin reads journalctl -xb and sees the failed dependency for the data mount.
Root is remounted read-write and the UUID is corrected from blkid, then mount -a runs without errors.
The server boots normally. The team adds nofail to optional mounts and tests fstab before reboots.

title: How a query is planned and run

steps.n: The client sends the statement text to the server.
The parser checks syntax and that the tables and columns exist.
The planner uses table statistics to estimate rows and cost for several plans.
It picks an index scan or a sequential scan, and a join order, based on the estimates.
The executor runs the chosen steps, asking storage for rows.
Storage returns pages from memory or disk, and rows are filtered and joined.
Results go back to the client. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimated against actual rows for each step.
Hundreds of application connections arrive at the pooler, most of them idle at any moment.
The pooler keeps a small set of server connections and queues requests when all are busy.
In transaction mode it lends a server connection only for one transaction.
The database runs the transaction and the connection goes back to the pool at commit.
The client sees its answer and its next transaction may use a different server connection.
If wait time for a free connection grows, demand is above capacity and you need to act.

title: Failure and recovery: idle transactions fill the connection limit
summary: Stuck sessions block new requests at peak.

steps.n: A handler starts a transaction and then calls a slow external service before it commits.
The session sits idle in transaction and keeps its connection slot and sometimes locks.
At peak more handlers do the same until nearly all slots are used by idle sessions.
The database refuses new connections with too many connections and users see errors.
Error rate alerts page the on-call engineer who sees connection errors.
pg_stat_activity grouped by state shows most sessions are idle in transaction from one service.
The engineer terminates the oldest idle sessions to restore service and notes the owner.
The team moves the external call out of the transaction, adds a timeout and a pooler, and alerts on pool wait.

title: One request through an LLM server

steps.n: The client calls the API with a prompt and settings such as the maximum tokens.
The server turns text into tokens. This runs on the CPU and can limit speed if it is slow.
The scheduler places the request in the waiting queue until there is room in the KV cache.
The GPU processes the whole prompt in parallel and fills the KV cache. This sets the time to first token.
Each step produces one token for every request in the batch, reading the weights and the cache.
Tokens are sent back as they are produced, and the request leaves the batch when it finishes.

title: How a pod gets a GPU

steps.n: The pod asks for one GPU as a resource limit.
The scheduler keeps only nodes that advertise a free GPU and whose taints the pod tolerates.
The pod is assigned to a node and the kubelet takes over.
The kubelet asks the device plugin for a GPU and receives its device paths and settings.
The container runtime mounts the GPU device files and driver libraries into the container.
Inside the container nvidia-smi lists the GPU and the model server can use it.

title: Failure and recovery: the model server crashes under load
summary: Cache runs out and a long request breaks it.

steps.n: Several users send long prompts at once after a product launch.
Each request needs KV cache, and the cache usage rises towards 100 percent.
A new request needs a block that is not free and the GPU raises an out of memory error.
The server returns errors or restarts, and users see timeouts.
Alerts for restarts and error rate fire. Time to first token had been climbing for an hour.
The engineer sees cache usage near 100 percent and a long waiting queue before the crash.
The engineer lowers the maximum context length and concurrency and adds a replica.
The team alerts on cache usage above 85 percent and on queue time so it can scale before a crash.
The user sends a token with the request. Nova checks it, checks quota and records the server in the database.
A message on the queue asks the scheduler to choose a host.
Placement shows hosts with room, filters remove unsuitable ones, and the best is chosen.
The chosen compute node receives the build request through the message queue.
The node downloads the image from Glance and asks Neutron for a port with an address.
The node starts the guest through libvirt and the state moves from BUILD to ACTIVE.

title: A packet from the internet to a server
summary: Floating IP, router and security group.

steps.n: The client sends traffic to the public address of the floating IP.
The router maps the floating IP to the private address of the server using NAT.
The port security group is checked for an ingress rule matching protocol, port and source.
If a rule allows it, the packet reaches the server. Otherwise it is dropped without a reply.
The operating system firewall inside the server also has to allow the connection.
The reply is translated back to the floating IP and returned to the client.

title: Failure and recovery: the message queue stops
summary: Every service reports errors at once.

steps.n: Logs fill the disk where RabbitMQ stores its data, and the broker stops accepting messages.
Nova, Neutron and Cinder cannot talk to each other through the queue.
New servers, ports and volumes fail or hang, and users see many different errors.
Monitoring shows errors in every service at the same time, a sign of a shared dependency.
rabbitmqctl cluster_status fails and the disk on the controller is full.
The operator removes old logs, restarts RabbitMQ and checks that the cluster is healthy.
compute service list and network agent list show every service up again.
The team adds disk alerts and queue depth monitoring and moves logs off the controller disk.
